important_note: These nodes preserve commonly taught named models as analytical/historical frameworks. Their inclusion does not elevate the models to universal factual laws. Exact qualification requirements remain course-specific.

nodes.title: Taylor / scientific management

teaching_content.core_explanation: Scientific management, associated especially with Frederick W. Taylor, sought to improve work through systematic study of tasks, standardisation, selection and training, clearer division of responsibility and performance-related incentives. Its enduring educational value is in showing how measurement, process design and incentives can raise consistency and productivity in repetitive work. It should not be taught as a complete or universally valid theory of people. Taylor's approach underweighted social relationships, autonomy, intrinsic motivation and many forms of knowledge work. Modern operations still use process measurement, standard work and continuous improvement, but these practices do not require accepting every Taylorist assumption about workers. A strong learner can therefore explain both the productivity mechanism and the contexts in which excessive fragmentation, close control or narrow incentives can create quality, motivation or adaptability problems.
teaching_content.why_it_matters: Taylor is frequently required by qualifications and provides a useful historical contrast between efficiency-focused and broader behavioural approaches.
definitions: scientific management: systematic task analysis and management system aimed at improving efficiency
standardisation: defining consistent methods or specifications
time study: measurement of task duration to analyse work methods
piece-rate incentive: pay linked to output quantity
important_boundaries: scientific management is not identical to all modern process improvement
standardisation does not require dehumanising work
financial incentives do not guarantee motivation or quality
Taylor is a model/history node rather than general subject truth about human nature
facts: Taylor promoted systematic task analysis, worker selection/training and clearer management-worker responsibilities
process measurement and standardisation remain important operational ideas
later management thought added social, psychological and systems perspectives
mechanisms: task analysis + standard method + training -> reduced variation -> possible productivity improvement
narrow output incentive -> increased measured output but possible gaming/quality trade-off
high task fragmentation -> specialisation benefits but possible monotony/autonomy costs
causal_relationships: standardisation -> consistency -> possible efficiency but reduced local discretion
examples: A repetitive packing process may benefit from ergonomic task study and standard work, while a product-design role requiring experimentation is less suited to tightly prescribed methods.
non_examples: Calling any use of data or KPIs 'Taylorism'.
applications: apply scientific-management logic to repetitive operations
compare efficiency benefits with people/quality effects
distinguish historical model from modern evidence-based management
real_world_transfer: Identify which parts of a modern workflow benefit from standardisation and which require judgement or autonomy.
assumptions: important tasks can be measured and decomposed sufficiently
performance can be influenced through standard methods and incentives
limitations: can oversimplify human motivation, teamwork and knowledge work; local optimisation may damage whole-system outcomes

misconceptions.incorrect_belief: Taylor proved that money is the main thing that motivates employees.
misconceptions.correction: Scientific management used financial incentives as part of a wider system; it does not establish a universal law of motivation.

interpretation: productivity evidence should be separated from assumptions about motivation
common_errors: assuming higher measured output equals better whole-business performance

uncertainties: Exact named Taylor content and terminology remain qualification-specific.

nodes.title: Maslow hierarchy of needs

teaching_content.core_explanation: Maslow proposed that human needs can be considered in a hierarchy, commonly represented as physiological, safety, social/belonging, esteem and self-actualisation needs. In Business education the model can prompt learners to look beyond pay and ask how security, relationships, recognition, autonomy and development may affect employees. Its value is heuristic rather than predictive. People do not reliably move through five fixed stages in the same order, several needs can matter simultaneously, and culture, life circumstances and individual differences affect priorities. The model should therefore generate questions about employee needs rather than provide a formula for motivation.
teaching_content.why_it_matters: Maslow is widely taught but is especially vulnerable to being presented as settled psychological fact. Correct treatment improves both motivation analysis and epistemic discipline.
definitions: hierarchy of needs: Maslow's proposed ordering of categories of human need
physiological needs: basic physical needs
safety needs: security/stability needs
social/belonging needs: relationship and belonging needs
esteem needs: recognition/status/self-respect needs
self-actualisation: fulfilment/development of potential
important_boundaries: the hierarchy is a theory/model, not a biological ladder
people can value several need categories at once
pay can contribute to several needs rather than map to only one level
satisfying a supposed lower need does not mechanically activate the next
facts: Maslow's model broadened management discussion beyond purely financial incentives
the strict ordering/universality has significant empirical and contextual limitations
mechanisms: unmet valued need -> possible motivational salience -> behaviour
work design/reward -> perceived need satisfaction -> possible engagement/retention effects
causal_relationships: employee context -> salient needs -> response to reward/job design
management intervention -> perceived need fulfilment -> possible motivation effect
examples: A secure, well-paid employee may value development and autonomy strongly, while another employee in the same role may prioritise predictable hours and social support.
non_examples: Assuming every employee must achieve one level before caring about anything above it.
applications: generate a broader set of motivation factors
real_world_transfer: Use the model as an interview or diagnostic prompt, then validate assumptions with actual employee evidence.
assumptions: need categories are meaningful enough to prompt discussion
limitations: weak support for a universal fixed hierarchy; cultural and individual variation; broad concepts are difficult to measure

misconceptions.incorrect_belief: Maslow's five levels are a proven sequence that every employee follows.
misconceptions.correction: The hierarchy is a classic model with substantial limits; needs can overlap and priorities vary by person and context.

evidence_of_understanding: describe categories without treating them as law
uncertainties: Exact diagram labels and required critique depth vary by qualification.

nodes.title: Herzberg motivator-hygiene theory

teaching_content.core_explanation: Herzberg's motivator-hygiene theory distinguishes factors associated with the work itself and positive satisfaction—such as achievement, recognition, responsibility and growth—from hygiene conditions such as pay, policies, supervision and working conditions that can create dissatisfaction when poor. The useful managerial insight is that removing a bad condition is not necessarily the same as creating engaging work. However, the two-factor separation is not absolute: pay, supervision and working conditions can influence positive motivation in some contexts, while individual and occupational differences matter. Learners should use Herzberg to analyse job design and reward choices, then test the theory against the actual situation rather than mechanically classifying every factor.
teaching_content.why_it_matters: The model creates a useful distinction between preventing dissatisfaction and creating meaningful/engaging work, while also requiring critical treatment of its evidence and categories.
definitions: motivators: factors in Herzberg's theory associated with the work itself and positive satisfaction
hygiene factors: contextual factors whose inadequacy may create dissatisfaction
job enrichment: redesign increasing responsibility, challenge or meaningful control
important_boundaries: hygiene factors are not 'unimportant'
pay is not incapable of motivating
satisfaction and dissatisfaction are not always independent continua
the model does not predict every employee response
facts: Herzberg emphasised job content and responsibility as well as employment conditions
the theory's factor separation and research method have been criticised
mechanisms: poor work conditions -> dissatisfaction -> retention/performance risk
job enrichment -> greater meaning/autonomy -> possible motivation benefit
causal_relationships: job/context factor -> employee perception -> satisfaction/dissatisfaction -> possible behavioural outcome
examples: Fixing an unsafe workplace removes a serious negative condition; it does not automatically make repetitive work interesting or developmental.
non_examples: Saying salary can never motivate because Herzberg called it a hygiene factor.
applications: distinguish removal of dissatisfaction from creation of positive motivation
real_world_transfer: When a retention problem persists after a pay rise, investigate work content, management, development and conditions rather than assuming the theory proves one cause.
assumptions: employees can meaningfully distinguish aspects of job content and context
limitations: factor categories can overlap; evidence depends on method/context; individual differences matter

misconceptions.incorrect_belief: Herzberg says pay does not motivate people.
misconceptions.correction: The model classifies pay mainly as a hygiene factor, but real responses are context-dependent and the classification is not a universal law.

evidence_of_understanding: apply to job design and evaluate limits
uncertainties: Exact factor examples expected in assessment may vary by course.

nodes.title: McGregor Theory X / Theory Y

teaching_content.core_explanation: Douglas McGregor's Theory X and Theory Y describe contrasting managerial assumptions about people at work. Theory X represents assumptions that employees tend to dislike work, avoid responsibility and require direction or control; Theory Y represents assumptions that people can find work natural, exercise self-direction and accept responsibility when conditions support it. The theory is best understood as a lens on management beliefs, not as two kinds of employee. Manager assumptions can become self-reinforcing: tightly controlling employees may reduce discretion and initiative, which managers then interpret as proof that close control was necessary. Conversely, delegation without capability, clarity or support can fail even when employees are willing. Appropriate management therefore depends on task risk, competence, motivation, accountability and context rather than choosing 'Y is good, X is bad'.
teaching_content.why_it_matters: The framework links assumptions about people to leadership, delegation, job design and culture and helps expose self-fulfilling management practices.
definitions: Theory X: McGregor's label for relatively controlling assumptions about worker motivation/responsibility
Theory Y: McGregor's label for assumptions supporting self-direction and responsibility under appropriate conditions
managerial assumption: belief influencing how managers design and control work
important_boundaries: Theory X and Y are not employee personality types
Theory Y does not mean no controls or accountability
a directive response to a high-risk situation does not prove a Theory X culture
the framework is conceptual rather than a validated binary diagnostic
facts: managerial beliefs influence control, delegation and participation
employee behaviour is also shaped by capability, incentives, job design and context
mechanisms: controlling assumption -> restricted discretion -> less initiative -> apparent confirmation
development + clear authority + support -> self-direction opportunity -> possible initiative/ownership
causal_relationships: manager assumption -> management system -> employee opportunity/behaviour -> manager interpretation
examples: A manager who requires approval for every minor decision may suppress initiative and later conclude the team lacks initiative.
non_examples: Labelling an individual employee 'a Theory X person'.
real_world_transfer: Ask whether low initiative is caused by employee unwillingness, lack of capability, or a system that gives no genuine discretion.
assumptions: managerial assumptions materially shape management practices
limitations: binary framing simplifies a wide range of motives, situations and management approaches

misconceptions.incorrect_belief: Theory X employees dislike work while Theory Y employees enjoy it.
misconceptions.correction: McGregor's framework concerns contrasting managerial assumptions, not fixed categories of employee.

models_frameworks: McGregor Theory X and Theory Y
uncertainties: Qualifications differ in how simplistically they label X/Y; reusable foundation should retain the more accurate assumption-based framing.

nodes.title: Lewin change model / force-field analysis

teaching_content.core_explanation: Lewin is associated with influential planned-change ideas commonly taught through a three-stage change model—unfreezing existing routines, moving/changing, and stabilising/refreezing new patterns—and with force-field analysis, which considers forces supporting and restraining a proposed change. In Business education these are useful structuring devices: the three-stage model prompts attention to preparation, transition and embedding, while force-field analysis prompts identification of stakeholders, incentives, capability, culture and other pressures that can help or hinder change. They should not be treated as mechanical recipes. Contemporary organisations often change continuously, forces interact rather than simply add up, and assigning numerical 'strength' scores can create false precision. A stronger application identifies the mechanism behind each force, asks which can realistically be changed, and considers unintended effects of strengthening or reducing it.
teaching_content.why_it_matters: The models provide accessible tools for analysing change while illustrating why named frameworks must be separated from factual claims about how every organisation changes.
definitions: unfreezing: disrupting/preparing to change established routines or norms
moving/change: transition toward new practices
refreezing: embedding/stabilising new practices
force-field analysis: framework identifying driving and restraining forces affecting a proposed change
driving force: influence supporting movement toward change
restraining force: influence resisting or limiting change
important_boundaries: three stages are a simplification, not a mandatory sequence in every change
force strength is a managerial judgement unless supported by evidence
resistance can reveal legitimate risks rather than irrational opposition
reducing a restraining force may be safer than simply increasing pressure
facts: planned change often requires preparation, implementation and reinforcement
stakeholder incentives, routines, capability and culture can enable or constrain change
continuous-change environments weaken the idea of a permanently refrozen end state
causal_relationships: change proposal + driving/restraining forces -> implementation behaviour -> adoption/outcome
reinforcement/system alignment -> persistence of new practice
examples: Introducing a new scheduling system may be supported by customer-service needs and better data but restrained by poor training, legacy processes and fear of workload monitoring.
non_examples: Giving each force an arbitrary score, subtracting totals and claiming the resulting number proves whether change will succeed.
real_world_transfer: Before a major process change, identify the strongest practical constraints and decide whether to remove barriers, build capability or redesign the change rather than merely communicating harder.
assumptions: material forces and routines can be identified well enough to inform planning
limitations: models simplify dynamic power, politics, emergent change and interacting feedback; 'refreezing' may be unrealistic in continuously changing environments

misconceptions.incorrect_belief: Force-field analysis can objectively score whether a change will work.
misconceptions.correction: It structures judgement about enabling and restraining influences; numerical scores are not objective probabilities or causal proof.

interpretation: force rankings are qualitative/ordinal judgements unless evidence justifies more; do not treat arbitrary scores as measurement
common_errors: adding arbitrary force scores as if they predict success

evidence_of_understanding: use the frameworks to structure change analysis
uncertainties: Qualifications may require one or both Lewin-related representations and may use different terminology; mapping should preserve exact course convention separately.
